title: What an AI detector can tell you
source: Karim Ibrahim · Language Testing in Asia · 2026

cues.text: Two essays look equally polished. One was written by a learner, the other with substantial help from artificial intelligence.
If a detector flags both, what has it actually established?
Karim Ibrahim's paper is a critical literature review of AI-assisted plagiarism in second-language writing.
It selected thirty-three of fifty-seven records. Its detector results come from previous studies.
Watermarking looks for a trace placed by a generator. A trained detector learns from examples.
Statistical methods look for patterns in text. Retrieval methods compare a passage with stored outputs.
These approaches depend on different kinds of evidence.
A false positive wrongly flags human writing. A false negative misses AI-generated writing.
An impressive score on one test set can hide errors when a tool faces another model, genre, or group of writers.
Ibrahim proposes three questions. Is the detector reliable? Do its results generalize?
And is the tool accessible in the setting where teachers would actually use it?
Use a flag to decide what to investigate. Review the drafts, and give the learner a chance to explain how they wrote them.
Make the integrity decision from the evidence in context.
